utterances.text: Yes, yes. It was already two or three months after the event, and I received instruction from Delalic. He was absent.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And were you in a position to question that instruction, to set it aside if needed?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Did you perform any investigation to come to that conclusion or to follow up on that instruction?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: I followed up on the instruction of my superior. He told me what to do, and I did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So how did you follow up?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: What do you mean, how I followed this up? Can you be more specific, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Did you write down what he said, or did you do any investigation, any investigative steps?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: No, no, I was not authorised to take any investigative steps. I could only have done those based on Delalic's instructions, not otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: With regard to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, let me understand something here, sir. Witness, are you saying what is written on this document was what you were instructed to write by Delalic, or he just told you to write something and these are your own words and ideas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I received instructions from Delalic, and I followed the instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What were the instructions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't tell you exactly, but there was an inquiry, a prior inquiry, whether there -- Croats had been killed, and there was a time limit for the answer. Delalic was absent. I asked him what to do. He told me to write that there were some dead people who had been killed during combat, that they were Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He told you those words that you must write? You must write that there were dead people who were Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And he told you to say that they were killed during combat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that they were killed in combat activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A question, sir, if I may, Witness. During combat activities against whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Between the BiH army and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Just a question relating to some of the details mentioned in that document. For example, it says, in the third-last sentence: "They were all dressed in uniforms." Was this part of the instruction you had, or did you have any physical evidence to that effect that prompted you to write this?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: This was upon Delalic's instructions. He was the one in charge of the matter. I never investigated the matter. I was never in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And it talks here about a burial location, Pjescara. Can I ask you, how did you get that information?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: From Delalic. I asked him what I should say, which places I should mention. He told me that these persons could be found in the Pjescara sector, which is a part between Maline and Bikosi.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If I show you a map, would you know where that place is?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: I sincerely doubt that you can show it on any map. It is a very small place between Maline and Bikosi. It would occupy not more than a tiny little millimetre on a map, so it's very difficult to show on a map, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Before you leave the subject, can we just ask the witness if you were involved in the burial of these 25 bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you have followed my words closely, I mentioned that no members of the army participated in the burial of these bodies. It was the Civilian Protection that was in charge of the sanitation of the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I noticed that, but my question was whether you had been involved somehow in the burial.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Would you be in a position to indicate at least the area where Pjescara would be located?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: On the map?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, show me the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If we could please use the from Map 10 from the Court binder, the bottom half of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we go to Map 10 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you go to Map 10, what do we do with that document, PT1584?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If this could please be tendered into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: PT1584 will be admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit 140.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now we have Map 10 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you indicate where that location is?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: It's approximately here [marks]. I know the place is called Pjescara.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you mark a "1" next to it, please.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you. What does the area look like that you have just encircled?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Well, it's a mountain pass between Bikosi and the Gornje Maline, and people used to dig sand here. It's not real sand but that's why it's called "Pjescara," meaning "the sand pit," and they used that sand for -- as building material. That's how the place got its name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could this map please be tendered?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The map is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be exhibit number 141.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Mr. Fusko, you stayed until March 1995 in the Military Security Service of the 306th Brigade. My question is: Was, at any point in time, an exhumation conducted?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Was there any time an on-site investigation by your Military Security Service conducted in the place called Pjescara?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: As far as I know, no. Whether someone in the higher superior command did something about it, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: My last question is: In October, when you wrote this report, did you have any witness statements or documents emanating out of Mr. Delalic's investigation which helped you drafting the report?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: No, the report was written after consulting him. I didn't have any report about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And did you have any witness statements dealing with the incident in Bikosi?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Any documents from Mr. Delalic being sent to the 1st Battalion of the 306th Mountain Brigade to inquire about this incident?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: I didn't have any such documents available. Delalic probably issued oral orders to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Did you find any documents authored by Mr. Delalic who were sent to the 3rd Corps about this, other than your own report, I mean, talking about the investigation?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Neuner. Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, Your Honours. I needed a little time.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Fusko.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Vasvija Vidovic, and I will be questioning you on behalf of the Defence of General Rasim Delic. Today, in the course of your testimony, I understood you to say that you had grown up in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The village of Dub?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you completed the secondary school for metallurgy in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That school did not provide you with any military knowledge, did it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: No, none whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Fusko, if I may ask you, could you please pause between my question and your answer for the sake of the record?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I understood you to say that when doing your regular military service, you only received very basic military training. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were not trained to do military police work at all, were you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: No, I wasn't, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of your career before the war, you had no contact whatsoever with police work?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You never worked on any kind of investigation until you were appointed to the security organ of the 306th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And this was in May 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: In April, in March or April, I was transferred to the security in the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying this. In other words, I understood you to say that you were given the military task of working on security matters without having had any experience in this area.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And in regard to your lack of experience, you were not an exception in the 306th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: In the 306th Brigade, it was not only I who was appointed in this manner, but I think only three or four men had any knowledge of military doctrine. There were only three or four such men.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the brigade had about 1.700 men?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't give you the precise figure, but it was around that number, between 1.500, 1.700.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Asim Delalic, your superior, the assistant for security affairs in the 306th Brigade, also had no military knowledge; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: It's my opinion he was not trained, except that he served in the former JNA as a military policeman, as far as I know, but only a military policeman.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Not a single person working on security matters in the 306th Brigade was trained to carry out these tasks; am I right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And the whole brigade had only one lawyer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And that was Mr. Haris Jusic, was it not?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: But Mr. Haris Jusic also had no experience in investigations; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes. Jusic was only a lawyer who had worked in a company as a lawyer before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And now, very briefly, I'll put a few questions about your brigade. The 306th Brigade throughout 1993 operated on the principle of a village army; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that in early 1993, the conditions in which the brigade was created were very poor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The 3rd Corps, you said, issued an order for the brigade to be established in late 1993?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This order from the higher command were not immediately complied with by all villages; for example, Gluha Bukovica, they simply did not want to be part of the 306th; then they went and joined the 314th?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes, Gluha Bukovica and I think the village of Zagradje or part of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you will agree that all of 1993 was a year in which there was chaos in your area when this brigade was being formed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes. In my opinion that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to show you a document. Your Honours, could the document D113 be shown.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Fusko, when the document shows up on the screen, please take a look at it. And, Your Honours, can we zoom in a little bit, so the witness can see. This document is a document issued by your brigade, the 306th, and it's dated the 8th of January, 1993. It is a report from the security organ, and it was signed by Mr. Delalic, whom you mentioned today. My question is the following: You may not have seen this document --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: No, I've never seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: -- but I want to ask you something about the facts mentioned in it. The document speaks about the situation becoming more complex in 1993, and it says the leadership of locals who held meetings and promised the soldiers zones of responsibility above their villages, and then it mentions insufficient information among the soldiers on the ground. Do you see that, insufficient weapons and equipment for the brigade?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes. Certainly, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And then you have this long paragraph, the one before the last, and it says: To be true, there are many cases of soldiers refusing to go to position. This problem is currently being resolved by the military soldiers bringing soldiers in and sending them to positions, and there have been many cases of military custody being imposed as a disciplinary measure." Witness, it's correct, is it not, that this document reflects the situation on the ground?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: I don't know how to explain this. This text shows everything. There was a situation of chaos. People didn't understand what an army was. In our opinion and according to our information, this was done because people were poor, there was a lack of uniforms, a lack of weapons, so people went to other brigades, as you just mentioned, the 314th, for example.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness. Your Honours, I wish to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be exhibit number 142.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you have just seen the document which shows that the military police of the brigade tried to restore order; am I right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your previous testimony, you've told us that only 20 members or around 20 members of the military police were part of your unit?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. It was not a full platoon, some 20 or so.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: None of them had weapons, did they?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: It happened on a number of occasions that military policemen went to bring somebody in, sharing one pistol or one rifle between two or three of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is true, is it not, that the commander of the 306th Brigade, with the few military policemen that they had, could not prevent this lack of discipline and people leaving the brigade?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: You're right in saying that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, I would like to ask you something about the military situation in that area. Your Honours, before I show the witness the document, I would like to remind him of one part of his evidence. You said that the Bila Valley was intersected -- it is the valley of the Bila River, is it not; am I right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It was broken up into four or five different regions by the HVO blockades?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes, starting with Stari Bila, Old Bila, and another one in there was a check-point there. There was a check-point in Baj [phoen], another one in Logor, one in Gornje Maline, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like the witness to be shown D114. This is a daily operations report of the 306th Brigade, dating 9 May 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to read to you a small part of this document. You can follow it on the screen yourself. Under number 2, it says -- "The Aggressor," under number 1, and under number 2, it says "The HVO." Please look at that second part. It says here: "On the 9th of May 1993, the HVO members continue to hold check-points and do not allow cars or civilians to pass. They confiscate motor vehicles." Is all this correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now I would like the Trial Chamber to understand. Please, Witness, help me. It is true, is it not, that the brigade itself was broken up, that it did not function as a single unity?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: To the Prosecutor's question, I answered that the brigade was divided into three or even more parts. So the functioning of the brigade was extremely difficult.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And now I would like to ask you something else, please. The brigade command did not function as one body for at least up to the 18th of June, 1993, after these combat activities?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you the date, but it didn't function. It may have started functioning maybe ten days after that, I wouldn't be sure about the date. In any case, it took some ten days for the brigade -- or rather the brigade command to merge.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Some of the parts had been in Krpeljici?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Others in Han Bila?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Not in Han Bila, but in Bila or in Han Runig [phoen] which is some two and a half kilometres from Han Bila. Some call it Han Bila, but the real name is the Bila Mine. It was located in the premises of the mine. .

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So the brigade command was split, it was not one body; am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Your Honours, I would like to tender this exhibit. Can it be given a number, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be exhibit number 143.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I would like to show you another document which concerns the event in the area where you resided. Your Honours, could the witness please be shown document D115. This is a telegram. The sender is the 306th Brigade, and the telegram was sent to the 3rd Corps. Your Honours -- witness, please, can you look at the first page? I would like the witness to be immediately shown the second page of this document to help us clarify a fact. Can the witness please be shown the second page of the Bosnian version. Witness, it says in the document "Gabela 710." Can you tell us what this means? What is "Gabela 710", if you know?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Then, Your Honours, can the witness be shown the first page of this document again? I will focus your attention to a small part of this document, where it says in the second line of this document: "On Tuesday and Wednesday the HVO and the Chetniks negotiated in the Vlasic sector, after which the shelling of Zenica and Mehuric, and so did the aggressor of an infantry fired, the HVO is grouping in the sectors," and so on and so forth. Witness, can you please clarify the following? This will also appear in other documents. The aggressor is the word that people in your neck of the woods used for the Serb forces; am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. The aggressor was mentioned as the Serb forces that were on the Vlasic plateau.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. "The Chetniks" is another expression that was used for the Serb forces; am I right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: You are right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, according to what you know, the document bears the date the 2nd of June, 1993. Did you know at the time that the Serb and Croat forces cooperated and mounted joint attacks against your area at the beginning of June 1993?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: I did not have any direct knowledge to that effect. And I don't know who sent this telegram. I heard from the local population stories that the Serb and Montenegrin aggressor, as we called it at the time, and the HVO members would meet usually at the contact points in the Vlasic plateau. I can't confirm that I ever saw that, that I ever witnessed that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: One moment, please. Yes, Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I don't wish to interrupt my learned colleague, but she has put a question, and this is line -- page 67, line 18 -- sorry, line 16, referring to the 2nd of June, 1993, and if I look at the document which is currently shown to the witness -- I just noticed that the translation is wrong. The translation said "22nd of June," which is displayed on the screen, and then it's a translation error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We don't see this "22nd of June" even on the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: It's in the middle under "Date." It says: "22nd of June," while the original, I apologise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can somebody point to "Date" on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: On the heading, there is a box saying "Heading." It says "306 Mountain Brigade." Below there, "Heading." Below the word "Heading" it says "Filed" and then "Date," and then it says, "22nd of June," and I was reading from that translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is the correct date?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: The correct date is 2nd of June, as my learned colleague has stated. I was just confused, myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And where do you see the 2nd of June or can you here?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: In the original, it says 2nd of June. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. You may proceed, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, earlier today, in answering my learned friend's questions about the events in Maline in June -- Your Honours, I apologise. Can this exhibit be given an exhibit number before I move on to my next question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. Before we do so, Judge Lattanzi is pointing at something. Would you like to say something, Judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: It is clear for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Do you have an objection to the admission of this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. To the Prosecution, the basis of admitting this document into evidence is not clear because the witness has said he doesn't recognise the document, or he has never seen it, and then on page 67, line 19, he says: "I can't confirm that I ever saw that, that I ever witnessed that." So the basis on which my learned colleague wishes to tender this into evidence is unclear to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may respond. I asked the witness about the facts that are stated in here, and I also asked him about cooperation between the Serb and Croat forces on the ground. The witness confirmed that he had heard about that cooperation from the local population, and this is the basis for the admission of this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Vidovic, can I just, for clarification, ask you about the basis upon which you seek to have this document admitted because in the transcript it reads that you asked him about cooperation between the Serb and Croat forces on the ground, but the document, I think, does not speak of any cooperation. It says that there were negotiations in Vlasica, but other than that, I don't see any reference to cooperation, and so, yes, can you please clarify?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the way I understand the document is that the two sides negotiated in the Vlasic sector, after which the shelling of Zenica and Mehurici ensued. At this moment, you may not find it clear. However, in order for heavy artillery shells to reach Zenica, they had to be used by the Serbs. Your Honours, it's no problem for me to withdraw this document and use it with another witness to avoid wasting time, but this time I have to say this: Your Honours, the witness has declined any knowledge about certain documents and declined having seen the document, and still the Prosecutor tendered all these documents for admission and these documents were given numbers for identification or were admitted. It's no problem for me to withdraw this document, Your Honours, but I don't think it's fair. Let me make myself even more clear. It is not fair to raise an objection being aware of the fact that the witness said for some of their documents, that he did not see them, that he did not know anything about them, and still they were tendered for admission. And then an objection is raised to a document of which the witness said that he did know something about the things that are mentioned in the document, and still an objection is raised about an admission of such a document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: You will realise, Ms. Vidovic, that the decisions on admissions of documents are extremely complicated, and they are not, therefore, easy to make. The rule we have tried to establish sets out that there has to be a relation between the witness and the document so that means that the witness must have either seen the document, or must have signed it, or must know about it. And if he doesn't recognise the document at all, then at least he shall be able to offer testimony about facts which are included in the document, and on this basis I guess we could probably admit the document into evidence. But, you see, this is a bit of a borderline case because the document doesn't exactly speak about the evidence that the witness gave, so we had questions. But if you're withdrawing the document and seek to introduce it through another witness, I think that would be the best thing to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you withdraw it, Madam Vidovic, I just want to add something. I think we need to be a little more correct about what we say about what has happened. There are two exhibits of the Prosecution which have been marked for identification this afternoon precisely because there was no clear basis for admitting them into evidence, and that was Exhibit MFI 138 and MFI 139. So maybe you are aware of others where there was no such definite relationship that was established, they may have slipped through the fingers, but those -- definitely those two exhibits were not admitted into evidence precisely because the basis had not been established. So it's not as if that there is a preferential treatment of the Prosecution here, unless you're talking about unfairness on the part of your fellow -- your colleagues on the opposite side by standing up to object. But I would encourage you not to withdraw this document or rather at best I suggest that you have it marked for identification, if you still have another witness to deal with it. Would that be okay? Let's do it that, so then. The document is marked -- may it please be marked for identification and could it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be MFI 144.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed, Madam Vidovic. I'm sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry, Madam. We have gone far beyond the time for a break. Is it a convenient time for you, or did you want to tie up something before we go?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, this is a convenient moment. I just wanted to say that the unfairness I mentioned was referring to my learned friends, not the Bench. I just wanted to make that clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I thought I'd heard you say so too. We'll take a break and come back at quarter to. I'm sorry we have taken ten minutes of the time, but we'll just have to do with 20 minutes. Thank you very much. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Fusko, we talked about that part of your testimony which referred to events in early June 1993. You mentioned that the event connected with Maline happened between the 7th and 9th of June, or at least that's what I understood you to say. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: I can't be very precise about the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In fact, this event of the 8th of June was preceded by fierce attacks by the HVO on the Muslim population of Central Bosnia as a whole; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: I don't know what you meant by "attacks."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I am referring to attacks by the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Roads had already been closed. That is some kind of maltreatment, because people were penned in by those check-points.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know of an attack on some Muslim villages in the areas of Maline, in the Maline area, before these events? Does the name of Velika Bukovica village mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could the witness be shown document D116.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, this is a telegram sent by the 306th Brigade. It's dated the 5th of June, 1993. It's brief. Again, it says "Gabala 210" and it's addressed to the commander of the 3rd Corps, and it says: "UNPROFOR should come to Velika Bukovica. There is one person seriously wounded. Ricice village is encircled and under attack." My question about the fact mentioned in this document is as follows: Were you aware that the village of Ricice [realtime transcript read in error"Kruscica"] was encircled and attacked on the 5th of June a little before these in 1993?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: At that time, I was at the forward command post at Vlasic, so I did not have any detailed information. But as I said a little earlier, you would hear things from people, from soldiers, who saw these things and then were at the line.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you hear that -- or rather you don't know anything about the events in Bukovica. All right. Thank you, Witness. Your Honour, on page 74, line 13, there's a mistake. Instead of "Ricice" it says "Kruscica." Let's clarify this. I asked the witness about the village of Ricice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let the record show, then, that it is "Ricice" and not "Kruscica."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will not seek to tender this document. I will put some -- the document can be put away.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I will put a question concerning your testimony about the Arabs, the Arabic fighters. You say that you saw them for the first time in the autumn of 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, you were able to observe that they were helping the local population, giving them food, for example? Were you able to observe that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: At that time?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the autumn of 1992.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Not at that time, but later on, maybe during the winter some of our people joined them, and then they were given food, weapons, equipment. But not right away, not as soon as they arrived.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. If I say to you that they distributed food to the local Muslim population, to refugees, for example, that would be correct, would it not?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you will agree that the Mujahedin very soon gained the favour of the local population?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: In my opinion, yes, but I couldn't tell you how many people thought well of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I won't ask you that. But testifying about the relations between the Mujahedin and your brigade, you said that your brigade did not cooperate with them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you had no communication?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In fact, it was very difficult to communicate with them because there was a language barrier, first of all; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You will agree that the Bosnian population -- that very few people in Bosnia speak Arabic; am I right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Only Muslim clerics, hodjas, imams?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Not even all of them; although, they know a little Arabic. But not all imams speak Arabic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. There were a few people who studied in Arabic countries?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: But these were few and far between in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And to the best of your knowledge, not a single Arab was a member of your brigade?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: I'm a hundred per cent certain that no Arab was a member of my brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Today the Prosecutor showed you a document concerning people going over from your brigade to joining the Arabs, that is. Your Honours, I'm referring to Document D135, and I would like the witness to see it again. I'm referring to Exhibit 135. It's already been admitted into evidence. Please put page 2 of the document on the ELMO. That's page 1. Could we see page 2, please. In connection with this document, I'll ask you the following: It's correct, is it not, that the 306th Brigade simply did not tolerate these people going over; am I right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The 306th Brigade tried to prevent this; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes, but without success.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Quite simply, the Arabs did not allow the military police to enter the camp; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And there was nothing you could do about it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Nothing, absolutely nothing, unless we were to enter into a conflict with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, when you mentioned the conflict, do you agree that at that time your population and your members of the army were already fighting two enemies; am I right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That would mean that at that point in time, in the same area, you would be taking on a third enemy?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Well, as you mentioned a little while ago had we tried to bring in those people who left with them, common sense tells us that a third front would have had to be opened up.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Now I would like to go back to this particular document. Please take a look on page 2, where the 306th Brigade mentions the difficulties, the failure of men to turn up at the positions, and you say that the judiciary did not assist you. So please try to recall that situation. You are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, if you don't mind, can we just hold that question? I just want to get clarity on the previous answer. Witness, when you say "Had we tried to bring in those people who left with them. Common sense tells us that a third front would have had to have been opened up," what do you mean? Who are these people, and bring them where to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was referring to people who left the brigade on their own initiative in order to join the Arabs. I'm speaking of Bosnian people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who had decided to leave there, the brigade -- okay, thank you very much. I have it. You may continue with your question, ma'am. The question was the judiciary not helping. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, let's clarify. Did I understand correctly that members of the brigade who left of their own accord, if you wanted to get them back, you would have had to enter into a conflict with the Arabs?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And for you, that would have been a third front in that area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now to go back to this document, please look at the bottom half of this second page. It says: "We can see from this information that not a single judgement has been issued in the Bila River valley, and the knowing about the inefficiency of the judiciary, soldiers are often committing offences bearing criminal responsibility." Witness, you are involved in security. It's correct, is it not, that in that period you wrote out numerous criminal reports and complaints to the judiciary?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Well, after the events, not in this period but later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Well, in the period starting in July or August of the same year maybe, and then for another year, so two years, more or less, in all.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. This document is entitled -- or rather is dated the 11th of May, 1993, and it says here that you do not have the support of the judiciary. In other words, I assume that before that, you had submitted criminal reports. But if you don't know anything about that, say so.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: I don't know. I know I worked on criminal reports afterwards in August or September. That was when I first started doing that kind of work.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But let me ask you the following: It's correct, is it not, that your brigade, let's say during the second half of 1993, wrote many criminal reports to the judiciary, and the prosecutor simply sent them back saying they were not properly written?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: I think you're right because criminal reports were sent back and never dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were told that they could not use them because they contained insufficient information and were not professionally compiled?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes, because we didn't have evidence and so the court rejected them.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was it the court or the prosecutor; do you know?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't say it was the court, but who within the court, I can't explain.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You don't know that; all right. Now, let me ask you the following: It's correct, is it not, that this problem of criminal reports being sent back was discussed at very serious meetings in Travnik; do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right, thank you. The Prosecutor asked you about people going over. You don't exclude the possibility that this happened after the order was issued on the establishment of the El Mujahedin Detachment?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right, I'll repeat it. You were asked about people going over from the 306th Brigade. You don't exclude the possibility that the brigade accepted this retroactively after the El Mujahedin Detachment was established; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Well, it's my opinion that this might have been at the end of August or in early September when they stopped talking about bringing those people in or, rather, getting them back. Whether somebody gave approval for them to remain with the El Mujahedin, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before that, there was a discussion of these people having to come back?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Well, that was a daily problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now I ask you to clarify something about the school in Mehurici. You lived near that school. It's correct, is it not, that the Mujahedin abandoned their accommodation in the school in Mehurici when that battalion of the 306th Brigade moved into the school?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes. They moved out to the camp in Poljanice, and they had room again on the third floor or in the attic, where they would occasionally come but not often.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: There was some food there, logistics?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Food, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Today you spoke in detail about how it was very difficult to get information from the Arabs; am I right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You, yourself, said that you personally could not tell the Arabs apart, they all looked alike?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes, they all looked alike, for the most part. They were dark-skinned, they wore long beards.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you are no exception; people -- local people could not distinguish among them, they couldn't say who was from Egypt, who was from Algeria, they called them all Arabs?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes. People call them Arabs, Mujahedin, but mostly they were referred to as Arabs.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that at one point in time an order was issued for the El Mujahedin Detachment to be established, and I want to ask you the following about this: If I were to say that in Central Bosnia and in your area there were Arabs who never joined El Mujahedin, would you accept that or would you say you don't know?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Well, I would accept that, but I would say it was a very small percentage.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Well, there were individual Arabs who, after a year or more, were not under the control either of the army or the El Mujahedin Detachment. On one occasion, I was given the task to make sure that a mass could be celebrated, so I went to in front of their camp, where I was met by one of their people, I think they said he was an emir, I'm not sure what their titles were, but that was already 1995, and they said that they could answer for their men except for one called Abu Hamza in Guca Gora. I think that's what you were asking me about.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So in that narrow area of Guca Gora, for example, there were Arabs who were not members of El Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Well, I know only about this one who was in Guca Gora.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You testified about Croat civilians who were accommodated in the school in Mehurici. You said that they left the school. Do you agree with me that when these civilians arrived, the Arabs were no longer in that school, they were in their base in Poljanice?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes, they were in their base in Poljanice because, as I said, in late 1992 they moved out of the school.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you agree that looking after the civilians was not within the competence of the army?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite true.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It was for the Ministry of Interior to deal with that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes. You mean their security? Yes, it was the Ministry of Interior and the police department that had their headquarters in Mehurici who were in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll go back to the civilians who arrived in the school in Mehurici. It's correct, is it not, that they were guarded by civilian policemen?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It's also correct that the 306th Brigade provided several military policemen to assist?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. They were from the Military Police Platoon, and they were at the lines facing the Serb-Montenegrin aggressor. On their way back from the line they stayed in Mehurici, and we asked them to help in order to make sure that things went well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does the name "Biban" mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting. It's just that I thought I should clarify the answer that the witness gave to your question about who escorted the civilians back to Mehurici, because when I asked the witness that same question, he said they were soldiers of the ABiH. So was it --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you asked who escorted the soldiers to the school. My question was: Who guarded the civilians while they were staying at the school? I think these are two different things, and I didn't see how my question entered the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'll go back to my question. Does the name "Biban" mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: I know a Biban from the area of our valley. He was a member of the Ministry of the Interior at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, he was a civilian policeman, not a military policeman?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Witness, you told us in your testimony that Haris Jusic was a lawyer in the brigade?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that you testified to the Prosecutor in October 2006?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have the statement here, if need be, but first let's hear what the witness has to say in order not to waste time.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember saying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a second. The transcript says he testified to the Prosecutor. Is it testified or did he give a statement to the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He gave a statement. He gave a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: To the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you remember that you said that Haris Jusic took statements from Croatian villagers from Maline; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, is it? Not?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know what happened to the statements afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let's proceed slowly, please. You also said that at the time the Croats were not willing to talk about the event; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Just go slow, Witness, for the transcript to catch up. It's correct, is it not, that they were afraid and that they didn't talk a lot about it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: If I suggest to you that military policemen of the battalion of the 306th Brigade who were involved in these events gave statements, would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: What event are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the village of Maline on the 8th of June.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: That military policemen were involved in that?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. Please, Witness, slow down. I'm not saying they were involved. What I'm saying is the following: If I were to say that military policemen or people from the 306th Brigade who escorted these people to Mehurici made statements, would I be correct? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: I don't know about statements made by them.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You personally maybe don't know about it. Will you allow for such a possibility?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: That they would give statements?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that they gave statements to Delalic or to Haris Jusic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Well, it's possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And it's possible that you don't know about it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Well, I certainly don't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It's correct, is it not, that on the 8th of June and for a period after that, Mr. Esad Sipic was the brigade commander; you said that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Esad Sipic was the commander at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that in October 1993, he was no longer the commander but was replaced by Vezir Jusufspahic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so, only I don't know the precise date.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. And you know, don't you, that from June until October 1993, the deputy commander of the 3rd Corps, Dzemal Merdan, visited that area?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes, he did; although, I didn't meet him myself. I didn't receive him, but I know that he came by.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know that he came by with representatives of the International Community?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: I know that they were foreigners, but I can't tell you what organisations they belonged to. I replied in the same way to your colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me go back to the document that was -- just to save the time, Your Honours, Exhibit 140. This is a short report that you sent about the event, and you confirmed that you actually signed that document. You said that you had received instructions from Mr. Delalic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, if I put it to you that that instruction referred mostly to the fact that members of the BiH Army did not commit the massacre, would I be correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so. This is what I tried to explain when the gentleman here asked me about the document. This is precisely what the document states.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now, Your Honours, I would like the witness to look at a document which at this moment, on the face of it, does not have much to do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question. I apologise, Ms. Vidovic. Witness, earlier on you told us, if I'm not mistaken, that the document that you yourself signed, you drafted this document pursuant to very precise instructions of your superior and that's how I understood it. Maybe I'm mistaken. It appears that this is a report that your superior provided, and now you're telling us that -- actually, what are the facts that are related in that document, and the document means that no members of the BiH Army committed that massacre. Do you now confirm that this is indeed the fact? I just need to be clear on your thoughts with regard to this document, because initially I understood your evidence differently.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About this document, this is about the army, members of the army, that they did not commit this massacre. This is what I had in mind, and this is precisely how I responded to the original question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where in this document does it say that the members of the army did not commit the massacre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A reference was made to the army, because this report was sent as a follow-up to a previous query.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Wait a minute, Mr. Witness. The lawyer asked you a question, whether it can be said that this document says that members of the army did not commit the crimes, did not kill the people, and you said that's precisely what you were trying to explain earlier, that this is what the document says. I'm trying to find the line, and once I find it, I'll show it to you. My question to you is: Where in this document does it state that members of the army did not commit the massacre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It doesn't say that in the document. However, what was meant by the document was members of the army, because our control was only over the army and nobody else. This is what is implied by the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't know where you get that implication. Just quote me a sentence or a paragraph in that letter which gives you that impression, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have the question in front of me. This is page 87, line 21. I was talking about Mr. Delalic's instruction, that this instruction was relative to the members of the army. This was what I put to the witness. I never mentioned the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Wait a minute, wait a minute, ma'am. Wait a minute, ma'am. You're at page 87. Now, I know that there are two versions here, but my line 24 says: "Q. Please, if I put it to you that that instruction referred mostly to the fact that members of the BiH Army did not commit the massacre, would I be correct?" Now, this is after you have asked earlier: "Q. Let me go back to the document that was just to save the time, Your Honours, Exhibit 140. This is a short report that you sent about the event, and you confirmed that you actually signed that document. You said that you had received instructions from Mr. Delalic; is that correct?" "A. Yes, that is correct. "Q. Please, if I put it to you that that instruction referred mostly to the fact that members of the BH Army did not commit the massacre, would I be correct?" Now, I don't know -- I don't understand that question. This witness told us that he received instructions to write this report in exactly the way that it is said. What he said here was what he received from Delalic. How the instruction to write what is written here can be interpreted to refer to the fact that members of the BH Army did not commit the massacre, I would like to understand because I don't pick it up from this document. And I may be slow on the uptake, but I would like you to help me.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But I was asking this question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, but I want one thing to be clear for the record. I may have somewhat broader knowledge, and I'm entitled to put in my case to the witness, and I put it to the witness that he had received instructions that was relative to the BiH Army. Your Honours, you may allow me to have some broader knowledge of the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam, we don't dispute that. We don't dispute that you have broader knowledge, but we need to understand step by step what is taking place. Now, when a witness gives an answer which is not apparent from the document, I ask him to explain. I'm not questioning your question. You put your question, but let the witness tell me, in response to this question by you, that the instruction referred mostly to the fact that members of the BH Army did not commit the massacre. He must tell this Court where he gets that from this document. And you have your broad questions, ask your broad questions, but before you get to that broad question let us understand so that we are with you where you go. Sir, where do you get it from given the fact that this is not your original document. This document, you were given instructions to write it in the manner which it is written, where do you get it from this document that the instruction had referred to the fact that members of the BH Army did not commit the massacre? And refer me to a passage in this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I received instruction from Delalic, as I've already told you. The meaning of the text, it is meant here that the army did not commit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where is that said, though, where is that said in this document that the army did not commit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It doesn't say so in the document, but the document was drafted in that sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How do you know that, sir, because you were just writing what you were told to write. How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're not answering my question. My question is: How do you know that? Because what you wrote here, according to your testimony, is what you were told to write. How do you then begin to see beyond what you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'm afraid I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You answered before I finished. My question to you is: How do you know that that is what was meant when that was not communicated to you and it is not in the document, and this document is the result of strict instructions from Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know how to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed, you wouldn't. You wouldn't know how to answer it. And if you did know, you would tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My opinion at this moment is that I can't provide you with any further information. The word "BiH Army" is not in the text, but the document originates from the BiH Army, and I was of the opinion that the text refers to the BiH Army; although, it is not explicitly given in the text itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Listen, sir, this document says "Clearly during a battle with units of the HVO in the villages of Maline, Bikosi, and Postinje, the HVO suffered losses in manpower and materiel and technical equipment as a result of the combat operations." Now, can you, from that paragraph, infer that the BH Army was not involved? Can you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not from this text. However, the fact that the document was drafted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean by "the fact that the document was drafted, therefore the BH Army was not involved." The next paragraph says: "In the above-mentioned area, dead bodies of 25 Croats were collected in the period between 8th June and 10th June 1993. The bodies could not be identified as they did not have any identification documents on them. They were all dressed in uniforms. The bodies were all buried at the location called Pjescara between Bikosi and Maline villages. We repeat that all these individuals died in combat." Where do you get the impression, from that reading, that the BH Army was not involved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in my opinion, the conclusion is very clear, the army didn't do it. And according to Delalic's knowledge that he collected from the people who had been there. Now, as who was there, I don't know. I never met those people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you let this Trial Chamber into how you come to that conclusion, sir, because we don't know how you come to that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot word an answer to that. I have told you that this referred to the army reports, and my superior told me that these crimes had not been committed by members of the army. As for the rest of it, I wouldn't be able to give you anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are now telling us new evidence. You never said so earlier and that is not in this letter. You haven't written in this document that [indiscernible] told that the army was not involved, and the question would be: Why didn't you do that, sir, if that is what you were instructed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in my conversations with him, from his stories, and actually he told me precisely to word the document the way I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed, and not to add anything else other than what has been written here, other than what's written here, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, why do you now want to add things that he didn't tell you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it is my opinion that this was not done by members of the army, actually based on my earlier --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me tell you something. We ask you to tell us facts, to the best of your knowledge, not your opinion. Okay? Please don't give us your opinion unless it is sought, and it will be sought under correct circumstances. You may proceed, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do have the right to put my case to the witness, to put to him my assumptions. And in keeping with Rule 90 (H), I have the right to inform the witness about my view of the case. And I also believe that the witness has the right to answer the way he wants, the way he perceives my questions. Thank you very much, Your Honours. And, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You don't have the last word. I told you it is your right to do so. It is our duty to understand his answers in the light of the questions you put to him, and if we don't, we must ask. Okay, you may proceed and ask your questions, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, earlier today you saw a document which was Exhibit 134. Can this exhibit be shown to the witness again, please? Witness, could you please look. This is a document dated 14 May 1992 -- 1993 of the 306th Brigade. This has already been shown to you by the Prosecutor. Please look at the part where it says "Remark." It says -- or "Note": "The 1st Mountain Battalion. The strength of one mountain company is in reserve and [indiscernible] 7th Muslim Brigade Platoon." With this regard, I would like to ask you this: It is true, is it not, Witness, in that area the 7th Muslim Brigade did not have an organised unit, but rather that it actually, in the village of Kljaci, there were some of the members who happened to be there at the blockade due to combat activities; am I right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: I know that it did not exist in the area. I don't know whether there was anybody in Kljaci, I wouldn't be able to tell you if there were any members there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, you don't know that the 7th Muslim was in the area?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: No, I don't, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now I'm going to ask you -- we will no longer need this exhibit, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It will be removed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness now please be shown Exhibit number 90.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you please take another look at this document? This is a document dated 28 May 1993. I want to ask you this: The title of the document is "Official Note of the Death of Brkic, Sakib." Do you know that person?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: The deceased?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is true, is it not, that that person had not belonged to the 306th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: No, he was a minor.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Witness. Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Just a few questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Witness, how many soldiers were in the 306th Brigade in 1993? Let's say June 1993.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Brigade members?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly. Between 15 and 1,700, around 1.600, but I wouldn't be able to give you the exact number because I did not have any insight into the personnel situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: In your evidence today, you mentioned you saw a couple of times Mujahedin. What was the largest group of Mujahedin you saw in 1992 in the Bila Valley? And I'm talking about locals and foreigners.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Between 50 and a hundred foreigners. And as for locals, there may have been up to 50. I don't know the exact number. I never counted heads but that would be the rough figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And where about would you see these people in 1992?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Mostly in the early morning. These people exercised. They would jog along the road from Mehurici towards Gluha Bukovica and other villages. They would run along the asphalt road to keep fit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If I may show you a picture. This is Exhibit 92, and page 6 of it. The ERN number, to help the Registrar, 0471-7268. Have you ever seen that person?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Possibly, but I can't be certain. I can't say I know who it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't see how these last two questions can arise from my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I agree entirely with you. Can you explain why you're asking these questions, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was yesterday showing the same picture to this witness, and he had just said he has seen a group of Mujahedin doing exercises, and yesterday I got additional information pointing to that person. I just wanted to follow up how many people he has seen. I take the point by my learned colleague, and I am prepared to go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Objection upheld.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: What was the largest group of Mujahedin you saw in 1993 until June?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you the number. The local people joined them, but there were around 50 of them, but I can't tell you the number. There was a group of between 50 and a hundred.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: A group of 50 up to 100 Mujahedin, locals and foreigners, in total?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes, yes, both at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: From a military perspective, what do you think can a group of 1.000 soldiers do with a group of up to 50 to 100 persons?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic is on her feet. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I object and I have the same objection as before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Neuner. Since you started your examination, I haven't seen anything that arises from cross-examination, and I must agree with Madam Vidovic, unless you can convince us to the contrary how these questions arise from cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, my learned colleague has put, if I can put it in quotation marks "the third front" argument to this witness, and I'm just trying to establish who was -- how many soldiers were on one side and how many soldiers were in a maximum on the so-called third side or third front side. This is all I'm trying to do based on the questions put before by my learned colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think you must then deal with the question of fronts, and then if your question of numbers of Mujahedin has to come in, let them come in in the context of dealing with the number of fronts. But your colleague never raised any questions about the strength of Mujahedin, per se. She raised questions about the number of fronts that the Muslim army would have been faced with if they had attacked Mujahedin. There would have been three fronts. Contextualise your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I agree with Your Honour. What I tried to do was just follow up on that suggestion by my learned friend and trying to establish some facts about her suggestion. That's all I'm trying to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Start from what was done in cross-examination. Then your learned friend won't keep standing up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I have asked a few factual questions. I think the witness has responded to my questions, and the Prosecution doesn't have further questions at this point in time. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I'll bring you back to Exhibit 140, because there is still something that I don't understand about the meaning of this document. So if the Registrar will please find it and give it back to us on the screen. And while the Registry is working, I'd like to put the question to you about what the purpose of this document was. Now, when I read it, I get the impression that ABiH forces were engaged in a combat situation with Croatian forces and that during these combat actions 25 Croats were killed. They were all combatants, and we can see that by the fact that they were dressed in uniforms. And it is further reiterated by the remark at the end of the data that all these individuals died in combat.
