So from the reading of this text, one would assume that nothing had gone wrong, this was a perfectly legitimate situation where 25 soldiers of the foreign forces were killed and subsequently collected. Yet you also told us that you had been ordered to write this by Delalic, and you informed us very clearly that crimes had been committed. So I cannot help thinking that this was a cover-up, this was written deliberately to hide the truth. And you knew the truth because you told us that crimes had been committed. I can refer you to the place, if you wish. So you knew, I suppose, at the time that what was written in this report was not the truth. The truth was that crimes had been committed, and if I may interpret your answer, and feel free to correct me if I'm wrong, the crimes were committed by the Mujahedin. Is this a correct assumption? I don't want to lead you anywhere. I don't want to pull tricks on you, so you have to tell me if this is how it was. I take it from your nodding that you agree. Now, my question to you is: Why was it so important to pass up a message to the 3rd Corps that no crimes had been committed? You knew that crimes were committed by the Mujahedin, possibly. Delalic knew. But why, then, did you not say so, and why was it important to keep your hands over the Mujahedin? You could have said that the Mujahedins were engaged in combat and 25 people were killed, but you didn't even do so. You said that it was the ABiH that had been involved in combat and 25 Croats had been killed. So tell me about, you know, why was this a cover-up, why was it important to not tell the truth here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was no cover-up. There were 25 corpses. That was well known. And as far as Delalic's information went, this was done by the Mujahedin according to what he found out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But why didn't you say so?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: I did say that when the colleague across the way asked me. They were kidnapped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Sure, but nevertheless in the report that Delalic told you to write, it appears nowhere in this report that the crimes were --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: No, not in this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And why not? Why did you wish to give -- or why did Delalic wish to give the impression to the 3rd Corps that no crime had been committed?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Well, this was about the army. The army did not commit anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But nevertheless it seemed as if you are taking responsibility for the killing of the 25 Croats. These were people who were killed by members of the BiH during combat, and the killed persons were combatants so that was all legal and lawful; yet you still tell me that these were crimes and they were committed by Mujahedin. So there is obviously something that is inconsistent, and my question is: What was Delalic's interest in passing up a wrong message to the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: I can't explain what he thought. Maybe in this context, the way this is written, and the instructions that were given, the idea was that it wasn't members of the army who had committed anything because at that time the Mujahedin were not under our control. Maybe that's what he thought, but I can't really explain what he thought. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Didn't you talk about it? I mean, it must have been the talk of the camp in these days.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: Yes, it was the talk of the camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So the correct version would have been to say that the members of the Mujahedin had killed these 25 Croats and that possibly a crime had been committed because they were not all combatants, they were not all dressed in uniforms; that would have been the true story. And so why couldn't Delalic have just say that? He wouldn't be held responsible anyway, nor would the 306th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to round off this point, these 25 Croats mentioned in this document that you signed and which you drew up according to the precise instructions of your superior, Delalic, according to your knowledge these 25 Croats, were they civilians or fighters? I need to have this finally clarified.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: I'm telling you again, I did not investigate this myself, and I cannot tell you whether they were all in uniform or not and whether they were all HVO members or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, you wrote down things of which you knew that at least partially they were not true, that they were false?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: No, because it was not I who investigated this, so I couldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: But you have also told us that you yourself did not know whether they all had been wearing uniforms or not. It seems that you wrote down things that at least partially were not correct, because you yourself say that you put it in the document that they all had uniforms. In any case, I understand the matter better than before. I have some other questions - I apologise - to you. Do you know that any of -- your superiors who were present in the area, did you tell your superiors at a higher level that the accused or somebody subordinated to the accused about the presence of foreign military in your area of responsibility? Did you tell anybody about that? Because the authorities who were not in the zone, you were there, you were on the ground, and you were the one who had seen them. My question is, then: Did you tell anybody about that presence on the ground? That presence, at least according to you, was not something that could be considered a normal occurrence.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: The command was informed about that, and they knew that these people had created problems for us within our area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have also told us in your evidence that you could not exercise your coercive power against these fighters, that you didn't have any control over them, and you could not do anything against your co-fighters that decided to join those Arabs, as you call them, because they were too powerful. You did not have, yourself, the power to face these people, to confirm them. I apologise for sharing with you some of the observations that I have made during your evidence, that the Chamber has made, when you were answering the last question put to you by the Prosecutor, which I found rather fundamental. I would like to clarify one thing. What made you think that they were so powerful? What constituted, in your view, their power? Is it their number or something else? What made them so powerful?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: My opinion and my view of the situation on the ground was this: These people did not refrain from any measures. They could have even killed a Bosnian Muslim. There was torture on account of the women, on account of all sorts of things. That's why we could not -- we did not dare enter a conflict with them. And they were all armed, they all carried arms, whereas in our brigade not everybody carried arms. There were a lot of people who were on the lines without any weapons. For example, in a trench there would be two or three men and they would share just one rifle, and that was the main problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So what you're saying is that the superior authorities knew -- they were aware of the fact that these people were present, that these foreign fighters were present in your area of responsibility. Still, your impression was that that presence was, in a way, authorised by the political and military authorities of your country. Would you say that, that they were there under somebody's authority?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: I personally did not have that impression. I did not have the impression that they were our benefactors because I saw how they behaved. And as for how the authorities felt towards them, I really can't be the judge of that. I don't know what the political authorities thought of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not asking you about what they thought, what their views were. Your testimony is that your impression was that they were aware of their presence but that you had the feeling that they were there under either implicit or explicit authority of the higher authorities, that their presence was, in a certain way, authorised and legal presence, a legitimate presence; let me put it that way. Did you have that impression?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: As long as this was not covered by any order, my opinion is that this was not authorised, that their presence was not authorised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So what you're saying is that they knew, but they also didn't have the strength or power to intervene, to chase them out of the area, to somehow regulate their conduct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN FUSKO
utterances.text: I really don't know how to answer that question. I really don't know how to explain things for you to make them more clear. I, myself, don't really know where they came from, how they arrived. I really don't have an explanation for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
